title: B2B Wholesale E-commerce Platform
audience: A curious adult coming from a different field, with no assumed industry knowledge.
scope: How wholesalers and other trading companies sell online to business customers through a webshop platform, using Highbiza in the Netherlands as the running example. Covered: who is involved, key ideas such as customer-specific prices and ERP integration, a short history, a worked example, economics and challenges. Left out: logistics and warehouses in depth, marketplaces as businesses, and the internal technology of the platform. Geography: mostly the Netherlands and the EU.
learningGoals: Explain why a wholesaler's webshop differs from a consumer webshop.
Describe who uses, pays for and runs a B2B webshop platform.
Explain customer-specific pricing, ERP integration and building blocks in plain words.
Follow a trade order from search to delivery and name where it can go wrong.
Describe one real trade-off a platform supplier faces.

introduction.whatItIs:
A wholesaler buys goods in bulk from manufacturers and sells them to other businesses: installers, shops, restaurants, garages. For decades those customers ordered by phone, fax, email or through a sales rep. A B2B (business-to-business) e-commerce platform is the software that lets those customers order online themselves, at their own negotiated prices, while the order flows straight into the wholesaler's administration.

Highbiza, a software company from Hengelo in the Netherlands, sells such a platform. Since 2025 it belongs to Katapull, a Dutch group of commerce software companies.
introduction.whyItMatters: Wholesale ordering is repetitive: the same buyer orders the same screws every week. When people type those orders by hand, they make mistakes and cost money. Moving routine orders online frees staff for advice and exceptions, and lets the business grow without hiring an ever-larger order desk.
introduction.familiarComparison: It is like the online shop you use at home, but with a login that shows your company's price list - a bit like a members-only store where every member has negotiated their own prices.
introduction.whereComparisonBreaks: A consumer shop shows the same price to everyone and gets paid up front. A trade webshop shows different prices to different customers, often lets them pay later on invoice, must match the wholesaler's back-office system exactly, and is used by professionals who care more about speed and correctness than about pretty pictures.

participants.name: Wholesaler owner
participants.role: Chooses and pays for the platform.
participants.caresAbout: More orders without more staff, predictable cost, a supplier that will still be around.

participants.name: E-commerce or marketing manager
participants.role: Runs the shop day to day: pages, products, campaigns.
participants.caresAbout: Changing things quickly without waiting for developers.

participants.name: Operations or ERP lead
participants.role: Keeps stock, prices and orders consistent with the back-office system.
participants.caresAbout: Data that matches and changes that do not break things.

participants.name: Trade buyer
participants.role: An installer or shopkeeper who orders for work.
participants.caresAbout: Their own prices, fast reordering and reliable delivery.

participants.name: Consumer
participants.role: A private shopper on a retail or direct-to-consumer shop.
participants.caresAbout: Trustworthy payment, delivery choice, easy returns.

participants.name: Platform supplier (Highbiza)
participants.role: Builds, hosts, tests and supports the software.
participants.caresAbout: Many customers on one maintainable platform.

concepts.meaning: A price agreed with one customer or a group of customers, rather than a public list price.
concepts.example: A plumbing firm pays EUR 4.10 for a fitting that lists at EUR 5.00 because it buys in volume.
concepts.whyItMatters: If the shop shows the wrong price, the invoice will differ and trust breaks; this is the core of B2B webshops.

concepts.meaning: The unit price drops as the quantity ordered rises.
concepts.example: 1-9 boxes at EUR 12, 10 or more at EUR 10.50.
concepts.whyItMatters: Buyers plan order sizes around these tiers, so the shop must calculate them exactly.

concepts.meaning: The wholesaler's administrative backbone for stock, purchasing, customers and invoicing.
concepts.example: Exact Online, Microsoft Business Central or Logic4.
concepts.whyItMatters: The webshop must take its products, prices and stock from the ERP and send orders back, or staff end up typing things twice.

media.alt: ERP (enterprise resource planning) system: Exact Online, Microsoft Business Central or Logic4.
media.caption: The webshop must take its products, prices and stock from the ERP and send orders back, or staff end up typing things twice.

concepts.meaning: Software that automatically moves data between two systems.
concepts.example: Every five minutes, stock levels from the ERP are copied into the shop.
concepts.whyItMatters: When an integration silently fails, the shop promises stock that does not exist.

media.alt: Integration (connector): Every five minutes, stock levels from the ERP are copied into the shop.
media.caption: When an integration silently fails, the shop promises stock that does not exist.

concepts.meaning: A reusable piece of shop functionality that can be switched on for a customer.
concepts.example: Highbiza says it has over 100, such as a customer portal, staffel prices or extended filters.
concepts.whyItMatters: Reusing blocks keeps cost and risk down; every bespoke change makes maintenance harder.

media.alt: Building block: Highbiza says it has over 100, such as a customer portal, staffel prices or extended filters.
media.caption: Reusing blocks keeps cost and risk down; every bespoke change makes maintenance harder.

concepts.meaning: A private copy of the shop where changes are tried before they reach real customers.
concepts.example: A new checkout step is tested on a temporary web address first.
concepts.whyItMatters: It separates experimenting from selling, so a mistake does not stop orders.

media.caption: It separates experimenting from selling, so a mistake does not stop orders.

concepts.meaning: EU consumers may cancel most online purchases within 14 days without giving a reason.
concepts.example: A shopper fills in an online return form for a necklace they do not like.
concepts.whyItMatters: Consumer shops must make this easy; business buyers usually do not have this right.

historyNote: These turning points are simplified; they describe the Dutch context of the running example.

history.change: Trade orders were placed by phone, fax and through sales reps, typed into an administration system by an order desk.
history.whyItMatters: This manual pattern is what B2B webshops still replace today.

history.change: Open-source shop software such as Magento and WooCommerce made online shops affordable; many wholesalers built shops with agencies and plug-ins.
history.whyItMatters: Years of add-ons often left shops slow and fragile, which is why many later replatform.

history.change: The Hengelo company previously known as UWKM renamed itself Highbiza to focus on e-commerce and complex platforms.
history.whyItMatters: Shows the shift from general web building to specialised commerce platforms.

history.change: SaaS platforms with fixed monthly packages, managed hosting and standard ERP connectors became the norm for mid-sized traders.
history.whyItMatters: Buyers now compare predictable subscriptions rather than one-off projects.

history.change: Highbiza joined the Katapull group, which combines webshop, POS, ERP, marketplace, shipping, EDI, returns and (from October 2026) warehouse software.
history.whyItMatters: Webshops increasingly come as part of a connected commerce stack rather than standalone.

walkthrough.title: Monday morning at a technical wholesaler (fictional example)
walkthrough.setup: Fictional characters: Anna runs e-commerce at a mid-sized wholesaler of heating parts. Bram is an installer who buys there. Numbers are illustrative.

steps.title: Bram logs in from his van
steps.whatHappens: Bram opens the wholesaler's shop on his phone and logs in. The shop recognises his company and shows his prices, not the list prices.
steps.whyItMatters: Without his own prices he would phone to check, which defeats the purpose.

steps.title: He searches by specification
steps.whatHappens: He filters valves by connection size and brand and opens a datasheet to confirm the right part.
steps.whyItMatters: Technical products are easy to confuse; good filters prevent wrong orders.
steps.watchOut: If the product data in the ERP is incomplete, filters fail and he calls anyway.

steps.title: He checks stock and delivery
steps.whatHappens: The shop says 14 in stock and offers next-morning delivery. The stock figure came from the ERP minutes ago.
steps.whyItMatters: Promises must match reality; a stock-out after ordering costs him a job.

steps.title: He reorders his usual items
steps.whatHappens: From his order history he adds his weekly fittings in one click and places the order on account.
steps.whyItMatters: Routine reordering is where the time savings are.

steps.title: The order reaches the ERP
steps.whatHappens: An integration sends the order to the ERP, which reserves stock and later produces the invoice. A shipping label is created for the carrier.
steps.whyItMatters: No one types the order again, so the invoice matches the shop.
steps.watchOut: If the connection fails silently, the order sits unseen; monitoring must catch it.

steps.title: Anna changes the homepage
steps.whatHappens: Anna publishes a winter-service campaign page herself in the content system, after checking it in the test environment.
steps.whyItMatters: Marketing can act the same day instead of waiting for a developer.

walkthrough.outcome: Bram ordered in minutes without a call, the order desk handled none of it, and Anna ran a campaign alone. Success for the wholesaler means a growing share of orders coming in this way.

valueAndIncentives.title: The wholesaler saves effort and grows
valueAndIncentives.explanation: Every order a customer places online is one the order desk does not type. The wholesaler pays the platform a monthly fee plus a one-off setup fee.
valueAndIncentives.example: Highbiza's packages start from EUR 149 a month plus EUR 1,490 one-off and rise with product and order limits.

valueAndIncentives.title: The buyer saves time
valueAndIncentives.explanation: The buyer does not pay for the shop but gains speed and certainty; if it is slower than phoning, they will not use it.
valueAndIncentives.example: An installer reorders weekly items from history instead of waiting on hold.

valueAndIncentives.title: The supplier gains from standardisation
valueAndIncentives.explanation: A platform supplier earns more when many customers share the same building blocks, because one fix serves all. Custom work pays once but costs maintenance forever.
valueAndIncentives.example: Highbiza notes that a problem solved in one block benefits every shop using it.

valueAndIncentives.title: Group cross-selling
valueAndIncentives.explanation: Inside a group like Katapull, a shop customer may also buy ERP, shipping or marketplace software from sister companies, so connections between them have commercial value.
valueAndIncentives.example: Highbiza lists Logic4, Vendit, EffectConnect and DeliveryMatch among its integrations.

challenges.title: Keeping two systems in agreement
challenges.whyHard: Prices, stock and customers live in the ERP but are shown by the shop; copying data takes time and can fail.
challenges.tradeOff: Frequent syncing is accurate but heavy; infrequent syncing is light but stale.
challenges.example: A price change in the ERP at 9:00 still shows the old price in the shop at 9:30.
challenges.commonApproach: Standard connectors with monitoring and retries; their limit is that every ERP is set up differently.

challenges.title: Standard versus custom
challenges.whyHard: Every wholesaler believes its processes are special.
challenges.tradeOff: Custom features win the deal but make updates riskier and costlier.
challenges.example: A bespoke checkout step breaks after a platform update.
challenges.commonApproach: Turn requests into reusable blocks where possible and test custom work in staging; limits remain for truly unique needs.

challenges.title: Migration without losing customers or visibility
challenges.whyHard: Moving from an old shop means moving data, links and habits at once.
challenges.tradeOff: A fast cut-over is cheaper; a careful parallel run is safer.
challenges.example: Forgotten redirects make old product links disappear from Google.
challenges.commonApproach: Test environments, data clean-up and redirect plans; still, rankings can dip temporarily.

challenges.title: Serving businesses and consumers in one shop
challenges.whyHard: They expect different prices, payment terms and legal rights.
challenges.tradeOff: One shop is cheaper to run; two separate experiences are clearer.
challenges.example: Consumers need a withdrawal form; business buyers need payment on account.
challenges.commonApproach: Customer groups that switch prices and rules per visitor.

misconceptions.belief: A B2B webshop is just a consumer webshop with a login.
misconceptions.reality: Its core is personal prices, assortments, reordering and tight ERP integration; the login is only the entry point.

misconceptions.belief: Once the shop is live, the project is done.
misconceptions.reality: Updates, security, tests, integrations and content continue for as long as the shop exists.

misconceptions.belief: More custom features always mean a better shop.
misconceptions.reality: Each custom feature raises maintenance cost and update risk; reusable blocks often serve better.

takeaways: Wholesale webshops replace routine phone and email ordering with self-service at negotiated prices.
The shop is only as good as its connection to the ERP.
Platform suppliers balance standard building blocks against custom wishes.
Business buyers and consumers need different prices, payment and legal treatment.
Groups like Katapull bundle the shop with ERP, shipping, marketplaces and returns.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why would a wholesaler's buyer phone the order desk even though a webshop exists?
knowledgeChecks.answer: Because the shop does not show their own price or reliable stock.
knowledgeChecks.explanation: Customer-specific prices and accurate stock are what make self-service trustworthy; without them, phoning is safer.

knowledgeChecks.question: In the walkthrough, what would happen if the integration between shop and ERP stopped silently?
knowledgeChecks.answer: Orders would not reach the ERP, so goods would not ship and invoices would not be made.
knowledgeChecks.explanation: The integration is the hand-off between taking and fulfilling the order; monitoring is needed to notice failures.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why might a platform supplier push back on a custom feature?
knowledgeChecks.answer: Because it adds maintenance and update risk that standard building blocks avoid.
knowledgeChecks.explanation: A fix in a shared block helps all shops; a custom feature must be maintained separately.
